A bangle is a rigid, solid loop — picture a perfect circle, like a ring, but sized for your wrist. Unlike a chain or a thread, it does not bend or flex. It holds its shape completely.

Because it has no clasp, hook, or opening, you cannot "fasten" it. To put it on, you slide it over your hand and let it sit around your wrist. To take it off, you slide it back over your hand. This is what makes bangles different from many other wrist ornaments — no locking mechanism, just a smooth, unbroken ring.

Bangles can be made from many materials:

  • Glass — the colourful glass bangles extremely common in India
  • Metal — gold, silver, brass, copper
  • Wood — carved, painted, or plain
  • Plastic or acrylic — often brightly coloured, common in fashion jewellery
  • Bone or shell — in traditional or tribal styles

The material does not change the definition. As long as it is a stiff, circular ring for the wrist, it is a bangle.

Bangles are almost always worn in multiples. People stack several (sometimes dozens) on the same wrist. When they move, the bangles knock against each other and produce that characteristic gentle clinking or jingling sound — a sound strongly associated with bangles everywhere in the world.

A single bangle can also be worn alone as a simple, elegant piece.
Is a bangle the same as a bracelet?

This is where many learners get confused, so let's clear it up completely.

A bracelet is the broad, general word for any ornament worn around the wrist — chains, strings, beaded loops, cuffs, and yes, bangles too.

A bangle is a specific kind of bracelet — the stiff, circular, clasp-free kind.

So: all bangles are bracelets, but not all bracelets are bangles.

Think of it this way: "fruit" is the broad category, and "mango" is a specific fruit. Here, "bracelet" is the broad category, and "bangle" is the specific type.

Bangles are deeply embedded in many cultures, especially across South Asia (India, Pakistan, Bangladesh), parts of Africa, and the Middle East.

In India particularly, glass bangles hold strong cultural meaning. For many Hindu women, wearing bangles — especially red and white ones — is a symbol of marriage and good fortune. Breaking a bangle is considered inauspicious. In many Indian ceremonies and celebrations, bangles are gifted or worn as part of tradition.

In modern Western fashion, bangles are popular purely as a style accessory, worn by anyone regardless of cultural background.

• She slid a gold bangle onto her wrist before leaving the house.
  • The market stall was filled with rows of colourful glass bangles.
  • He gifted her a set of silver bangles for her birthday.
  • The sound of her bangles clinking echoed down the hallway.
  • She wore a single copper bangle as her only jewellery that day.
A bangle is a stiff, rigid, circular bracelet — with no clasp — that is slipped over the hand onto the wrist, made of materials like glass, metal, or wood, and commonly worn in multiples.
1459:
To banish someone means to officially force them to leave a place — usually a country, kingdom, or community — as a punishment, and to strictly forbid them from ever coming back. The key idea is: you are removed, and you are not allowed to return.

Think of a king pointing at a traitor and declaring, "Get out of my kingdom and never come back." That is banishment. It is not a request. It is not voluntary. It is an order backed by authority.

This word is used in two important ways:

1. The Literal Use — Forcing a Person Out of a Place

This is the original, most direct meaning. A person in authority (a ruler, a government, a court, a community) forces someone to permanently leave a territory as a punishment.

Examples:

  • The king banished the rebellious knight from the kingdom.
  • The emperor banished his political enemies to a remote island.
  • She was banished from her village after breaking its laws.

Notice that the person doing the banishing always has power or authority over the one being banished. A stranger on the street cannot banish you. But a ruler, a court, or a governing body can.

2. The Figurative Use — Completely Getting Rid of Something

This is equally common in modern English. Here, you are not sending a person away. Instead, you are forcefully and completely removing a thought, feeling, memory, or problem from your mind or your life. The idea of force and completeness still applies — you are not gently letting go of something; you are decisively driving it out.

Examples:

  • He banished all thoughts of failure from his mind before the exam.
  • She banished her fears and jumped into the water.
  • The doctor's good news banished his anxiety completely.
  • They opened the windows to banish the smell from the room.

In this figurative sense, you are the authority. You are the one with power over your own mind or space, and you use that power to forcefully expel something unwanted.

Several words seem similar to banish, but each one means something slightly different. Understanding these differences will sharpen your understanding significantly.

Banish vs. Exile
Both involve forcing someone to leave. However, exile can sometimes be self-chosen (a person might go into exile willingly to escape danger). Banish is always imposed by an authority — no one chooses to be banished. Someone else does it to you.

Banish vs. Expel
Expel means to force someone out of a group or institution (like a school, a club, or an organization). Banish is broader and more severe — it usually refers to a place or territory, not just a group. You expel a student from a school; you banish a criminal from a country.

Banish vs. Dismiss
Dismiss is much milder. If a teacher dismisses students, she simply lets them go. There is no punishment and no permanent restriction. Banish carries a sense of permanence and penalty that dismiss completely lacks.

Banish is not a neutral word. It carries weight. It sounds formal, serious, and final. When you use it, you signal that the removal is:

  • Deliberate — it is a conscious, decided act.
  • Complete — nothing is left behind; the person or thing is fully gone.
  • Permanent (or long-lasting) — it is not a temporary removal.
  • Authoritative — someone with power is making this happen.

This is why the word appears often in literature, history, law, and dramatic writing. In casual speech, people still use it — but always with that same underlying feeling of decisive, total removal.

Knowing the opposite of a word helps you understand its meaning from both sides.

  • Welcome — to invite someone in (the complete opposite of banishing)
  • Recall — to officially bring someone back (a banished person might later be recalled)
  • Reinstate — to restore someone to their previous place or position
  • Embrace — to accept something fully (the opposite of banishing a thought or feeling)
A Complete Set of Examples to Lock It In

Literal (person from a place):

  • The court banished him from the country for ten years.
  • After the war, the defeated general was banished to a remote island.

Figurative (feeling, thought, or thing from a space):

  • She banished the memory of that painful day from her mind.
  • A good night's sleep banished his tiredness completely.
  • Their laughter banished the uncomfortable silence in the room.
  • The new streetlights banished the darkness from the alleyway.

Slightly formal / literary:

  • The king banished the wizard from his realm forever.
  • With one firm decision, she banished all doubt.

To banish is to forcefully and completely drive someone or something away — and make sure it stays away. Whether it is a person removed from a kingdom by a ruler, or a fear removed from your mind by your own will, the act is always deliberate, decisive, and total.
1460: Banishment is the act of officially and forcefully sending someone away from a place — usually their own country, city, or community — and ordering them never to return. It is a punishment. The person is not just asked to leave; they are commanded to leave, and if they come back, they face even harsher consequences.

Think of it this way: you belong somewhere. You have a home, a community, a country. Banishment means that a person or authority with power over you decides you are no longer allowed to be part of that place. You are cast out. You lose your right to be there.

Three things are always true about banishment:

  1. It is forced. The person did not choose to leave. They were made to go.
  2. It is official or authoritative. It comes from someone with power — a king, a court, a government, a community leader, or a formal institution.
  3. It involves a prohibition on return. The person cannot come back. If they do, they are breaking the terms of their banishment and will be punished further.
What makes banishment different from simply being removed?

Banishment is not the same as being fired from a job, being asked to leave a party, or being deported (though deportation can sometimes overlap with it). The word carries a strong sense of permanent exclusion from a place that was once yours. It is a deeply serious, formal, and often irreversible action. There is a finality to it. The person doesn't just lose their home — they lose their right to belong.
Who imposes banishment, and on whom?

Historically, banishment was imposed by kings, emperors, governments, and courts on people they considered dangerous, disloyal, criminal, or politically threatening. A revolutionary might be banished. A traitor might be banished. A religious dissenter might be banished. Even famous thinkers and philosophers were banished from ancient cities for their ideas.

In older societies, being banished was considered a devastating punishment — sometimes even worse than imprisonment — because it meant losing everything: your family, your friends, your status, your identity, and your sense of belonging. You were cut off from the world you knew and thrust into the unknown, often with no resources and no support.

In modern times, banishment is less common as a formal legal punishment, but it still exists in some forms — such as exile orders, restraining orders that banish someone from a neighbourhood, or formal exile imposed on political figures.
The emotional weight of the word

Banishment is not a neutral word. It carries heaviness. When you say someone suffered banishment, you are saying they experienced a profound loss — not just of a place, but of belonging, identity, and home. It evokes images of someone walking away from everything they ever knew, alone, with no way to return.

This is why the word is often used in literature, history, and drama to describe tragic moments — the moment a character loses everything and is cast into the world as an outsider.

Beyond its literal meaning, banishment is sometimes used figuratively (not literally) to describe any situation where something is completely removed, rejected, or driven away with force and finality.

For example:

  • "With one decision, doubt was banished from her mind."
  • "The new law resulted in the banishment of certain practices from the industry."

Here, "banishment" just means the total and decisive removal of something. The tone remains serious and final — that is always the flavour the word carries.

• The king ordered the banishment of the traitor from the kingdom.
  • After years of banishment, she longed to see her homeland again.
  • His banishment from the city meant he could never see his family.
  • The court sentenced him to permanent banishment rather than prison.

• Banish (verb) — to carry out the act: "The emperor decided to banish his rival."
  • Banished (adjective/past tense) — describing someone who has been sent away: "The banished prince wandered for years."
  • Banisher (noun) — the one who banishes (rare in use).
Banishment is the formal, forced, and often permanent removal of a person from a place they belong to, as a punishment, with a strict order never to return.
1461: A banister is the railing structure along the side of a staircase — the thing you reach out and hold onto when you walk up or down stairs to keep yourself steady and safe.

This is where things get a little interesting. The word "banister" can refer to three slightly different things depending on context, and all three uses are correct:

  1. The handrail alone — the long, smooth rail running diagonally along the staircase that your hand actually grips and slides along. This is the part you "hold the banister" when you grab it.
  2. The vertical posts (spindles) alone — the series of narrow, upright pillars standing side by side underneath the handrail, supporting it from below. These keep the rail up and also act as a fence to stop people from falling through the open side of a staircase.
  3. The whole assembly together — the handrail plus all the vertical posts as one complete unit. This is the most common everyday use of the word.

So if someone says "the banister," they could mean any of the above. Context usually makes it obvious which one they mean. In most casual conversations, "banister" simply means the entire railing system on a staircase.

Picture a typical indoor staircase in a house. On the open side of the staircase (the side that isn't a wall), you'll see:

  • A long, smooth rail running at an angle, parallel to the slope of the stairs. This goes from the bottom of the staircase all the way to the top. That's the handrail.
  • Beneath it, a row of slim vertical rods or pillars, equally spaced, standing straight up from each stair step all the way to the handrail above. These are the spindles (also called balusters).
  • Often, at the very bottom of the staircase (and sometimes at the top), there's one thick, sturdy post that anchors everything in place. This is called a newel post.

All of this together — the rail, the spindles, and the newel posts — is what's commonly called the banister.

Banisters can be made of wood, metal (like wrought iron or steel), stone, or glass. In older or more ornate buildings, they are often beautifully carved or decorated. In modern homes, they might be sleek and minimal.

Banisters are found wherever there are stairs with an open side:

  • On indoor staircases in homes, apartments, hotels, offices, and public buildings
  • On outdoor staircases leading up to a building's entrance
  • On elevated walkways, balconies, or platforms where there's a risk of falling — though in those cases the structure is more commonly called a railing or balustrade rather than a banister (banister is most naturally tied to staircases)

A banister serves two main purposes:

1. Safety and support — Its primary job is to stop people from falling off the open side of a staircase. Stairs are one of the most common places where people slip or lose balance, especially children, elderly people, or anyone carrying something heavy. By gripping the handrail, you give yourself a stable reference point and can catch yourself if you stumble. The vertical spindles fill the gap underneath and act as a guardrail, preventing anyone from tumbling through.

2. Decoration — Banisters, especially in homes and grand buildings, are also a major design element. A beautifully crafted wooden banister with carved spindles can be the centerpiece of an entryway. Architects and interior designers put a lot of thought into the style of a banister.
How is the word used in sentences?

Here are some natural, everyday examples:

  • "She held onto the banister carefully as she came down the steep stairs."
  • "The child slid down the banister instead of walking down the steps." (Sliding down the handrail — a classic childhood activity!)
  • "The old banister was wobbly and needed to be fixed."
  • "The mansion had a grand curved banister made of dark mahogany."
  • "He painted the banister white to match the walls."
  • "Watch out — one of the spindles in the banister is broken."
A subtle point about related words

You may come across these words, so it helps to know how they relate:

  • Baluster — This is the precise technical word for a single vertical spindle/post in a banister. Multiple balusters line up to form the row beneath the handrail.
  • Balustrade — The formal architectural term for the complete railing system (handrail + balusters + base). "Banister" and "balustrade" overlap heavily in meaning. "Balustrade" is used more in formal, architectural, or historical writing; "banister" is more natural in everyday speech.
  • Handrail — Specifically the horizontal or angled rail you grip. A handrail can also exist without spindles (e.g., a rail mounted directly to a wall on a staircase). Every banister has a handrail, but not every handrail is part of a banister.
  • Newel post — The large anchor post at the base or top of the banister. Not a synonym for banister, but part of the same structure.
You may occasionally see it spelled "bannister" (with two n's). Both spellings — banister and bannister — are accepted and used. Neither is wrong.

A banister is the railing structure on the side of a staircase — consisting of a handrail you hold and the row of vertical posts supporting it — whose purpose is to keep you safe from falling and to help you move up and down stairs with confidence. In everyday English, when someone says "hold the banister" or "the banister is broken," they're almost always talking about this entire structure as a whole.
1462: "Banjo-eyed" means having eyes that are wide open and bulging — the way a person's eyes look when they are struck by extreme surprise, shock, or amazement. Think of someone who just witnessed something completely unexpected: their eyes shoot open as wide as they possibly can, and they might even seem to pop slightly outward. That look is what "banjo-eyed" captures.
Why does a banjo come into it?

A banjo — the musical instrument — has a large, round, circular body. When someone is banjo-eyed, their eyes resemble that round, prominent shape: big, wide, and striking. The word works as a vivid, slightly comic image. You picture the eyes almost stretching open to the point where they dominate the face, the way a banjo's round face dominates the instrument.

"Banjo-eyed" almost always describes a sudden, involuntary reaction. The emotion behind it is usually one of these:

  • Shock — something happened that nobody saw coming
  • Amazement — something so impressive or beautiful that the eyes go wide
  • Fear or alarm — something frightening appears without warning
  • Excitement or wonder — especially in children seeing something for the first time

The key idea is that the reaction is overwhelming enough that the person loses control of their expression. Their eyes just fly open.

"Banjo-eyed" is an informal, colloquial word — you would not find it in a formal essay or a legal document. It has a slightly playful or humorous quality. When a writer uses it, they are often painting a vivid, almost cartoonish picture of a person's reaction, which adds a bit of warmth or comedy to the scene, even if the situation itself is serious.

It is more common in American English, though it is understood in other varieties of English too.
How it is used in sentences

Here are clear examples showing the word in action:

  • "The children were banjo-eyed as the magician pulled a live rabbit from his hat."
    → The children were so amazed their eyes went completely wide.
  • "She stood banjo-eyed at the door when she saw the mess in the kitchen."
    → She was shocked by what she saw — her eyes flew open.
  • "He arrived at the stadium banjo-eyed, unable to believe the size of the crowd."
    → He was overwhelmed with amazement at something he had never seen before.
  • "The soldiers were banjo-eyed when the general walked in unannounced."
    → They were caught completely off guard, eyes wide with surprise.

Notice that in each case, the reaction is instant and uncontrolled. Nobody decides to be banjo-eyed — it just happens to them.
How it differs from similar words

You may already know words like wide-eyed, bug-eyed, or goggle-eyed — all of which describe a similar look. "Banjo-eyed" belongs to this family, but it is a bit more vivid and quirky than "wide-eyed," and carries a slightly more old-fashioned or folksy charm compared to "bug-eyed." All of them describe the same basic physical reaction, but "banjo-eyed" tends to feel the most colorful and expressive of the bunch.
If someone is banjo-eyed, their eyes are wide open and prominent — bulging with shock, surprise, fear, or amazement at something that caught them completely off guard.
1463: The word bank has several distinct meanings in English. Each one is its own separate idea, so think of "bank" not as one word with one meaning, but as one word that wears several different hats. Here they all are, explained fully.

This is the most common meaning today. A bank is an organization — usually a building or a company — that deals with money on behalf of people and businesses.

Here is what a bank does:

  • It keeps your money safe. You give it your money, and it holds it for you. This is called a deposit. You can take the money back whenever you need it.
  • It lends money to people who need it. When someone needs a large sum — say, to buy a house — the bank lends it to them. The person must pay it back over time, plus a little extra. That extra is called interest.
  • It acts as a middleman for payments. When you pay someone, the bank moves money from your account to theirs.

So a bank is essentially a trusted place where money flows in, is stored, and flows out — safely and in an organized way.

"She went to the bank to deposit her salary."
"The bank approved his loan application."

Related compound terms:

  • bank account — a personal record of your money held at a bank
  • bank balance — how much money you currently have in your account
  • central bank — a country's main government-controlled bank that manages the whole economy's money supply (e.g., the Reserve Bank of India)
  • investment bank — a specialized type of bank that helps businesses raise large amounts of money, not the usual savings/loan bank people use personally
2. The Edge of a River, Lake, or Other Body of Water

A bank is the ground along the side of a river, stream, or lake — the raised land that borders the water and keeps it contained.

Think of a river as flowing through a channel. The walls of that channel made of earth and soil — the ground on each side — are the banks.

"We sat on the river bank and watched the boats go by."
"The children played on the grassy bank of the stream."

You will often hear left bank and right bank — these refer to the two sides of a river when you are facing the direction the water flows.
3. A Raised Mound of Earth or a Slope

A bank can also mean a ridge or mound of earth — essentially a raised, sloping piece of ground. This is similar to meaning #2 but is not necessarily next to water.

"The workers built a bank of soil to stop the water from flooding the road."
"The car drove up the grassy bank on the side of the road."

You also see this meaning in the word embankment, which is a long, man-made bank of earth built to carry a road or railway, or to hold back water.
4. A Store or Reserve of Something

A bank can mean a carefully collected and stored supply of something — especially something valuable that will be used later when needed.

This meaning comes from the idea of a financial bank: just as a bank stores money, you can "bank" anything important for future use.

Common examples:

  • blood bank — a place where donated blood is collected, stored, and made available for patients who need it during surgery or emergencies
  • data bank (or database) — a large, organized collection of stored information in a computer
  • memory bank — used informally to describe the mental storage of a person's or machine's memories
  • seed bank — a place where seeds of various plants are stored to preserve them, especially rare or endangered species
  • sperm bank / egg bank — a medical facility that stores donated sperm or eggs for fertility treatments
  • food bank — a place that collects donated food and distributes it to people in need

"The hospital's blood bank ran low after the disaster."
"Scientists store rare plant species in seed banks to protect them from extinction."

The key idea: a bank in this sense is an organized, safe store of a resource that can be withdrawn when needed — just like money in a financial bank.
5. A Row, Cluster, or Arrangement of Similar Things

A bank can describe a group of similar objects arranged close together in a line or cluster — usually things that work together or belong to the same category.

"A bank of switches controlled all the lights in the building."
"The technician stood before a bank of monitors."
"A bank of clouds gathered on the horizon."

Think of it as a "panel" or "array." When many similar items are placed side by side in an organized way, that collection is called a bank.
6. An Elevated Area Under Water (A Sandbank or Shoal)

In geography and navigation, a bank refers to a raised area of the seabed or the bottom of a river that is shallower than the water around it. These are dangerous for ships because the water above them is very shallow.

"The ship ran aground on a hidden bank."
"Fishermen often gather at offshore banks because fish tend to gather in those shallow areas."

Famous examples: the Grand Banks off the coast of Canada are large underwater plateaus in the Atlantic Ocean, famous for their rich fish populations.

A specific type of this is a sandbank — a ridge of sand built up by the movement of water, found in rivers or along coastlines. Part of it may even stick out above the water's surface.

Despite how different these meanings seem, there is actually a common thread running through most of them: the idea of something raised, concentrated, or set aside.

  • A riverbank is raised ground along the water.
  • A mound of earth is a raised ridge.
  • A sandbank is a raised area of the seabed.
  • A financial bank is a concentrated, set-aside store of money.
  • A blood bank is a concentrated, set-aside store of blood.
  • A bank of switches is a concentrated cluster of objects.

Once you see this underlying idea, the word feels much less scattered and more like one coherent concept wearing different clothes depending on the situation.
Quick Reference: All the Senses at a Glance

MeaningWhat it refers to
Financial institutionA company/building that stores and lends money
River/lake edgeThe ground bordering a body of water
Raised mound of earthA ridge or slope of soil or earth
Store of a resourceA collected reserve (blood bank, data bank, etc.)
Row/cluster of thingsA lined-up group of similar objects
Underwater raised areaA shallow elevated patch of seabed or riverbed

That is the complete picture of "bank" as a noun. You now know every major sense of the word as it is actually used in everyday English, literature, science, and geography.
1464: "Bank" as a verb has six distinct meanings. They look unrelated at first, but each one connects to some idea of a bank — a slope, a pile, a border, or a place that holds things. Below is every meaning, explained fully with examples.
1. To deposit money / to use a bank as a customer

The most straightforward financial use. When you bank money, you put it into a bank account. You also use it to say which bank you use.

  • "She banked her salary as soon as she received it." (= she deposited it)
  • "I need to bank this cheque before the weekend."
  • "Which bank do you bank with?" (= Which bank do you use?)
  • "I bank with HDFC." (= I have my account there)

Extended financial use — you can also "bank" something non-monetary, meaning to store it for future use, the way a blood bank stores blood:

  • "The hospital banks donated tissue for future surgeries."
2. To rely on something / to count on it ("bank on")

This is one of the most common uses in daily conversation. When you are banking on something, you are depending on it, trusting it will happen or be available.

  • "Don't bank on the train being on time — it's often late."
  • "She's banking on getting a scholarship to pay for her education."
  • "I wouldn't bank on that if I were you."

Important nuance: "Bank on" very often appears in warnings or cautious advice, suggesting the thing you're counting on might not actually come through. The last example above is a classic way to warn someone that they are relying on something uncertain.

That said, it can also be used neutrally or positively:

  • "The team is banking on their star player to perform in the final."
3. To tilt sideways while turning (aircraft, cars, roads)

When a plane turns, it doesn't just point in a new direction — it leans or tilts to one side. This is called banking. The same word applies to racing cars and even roads.

  • "The pilot banked the aircraft sharply to avoid the storm."
  • "The plane banked left and began its descent."
  • "The racing car banked tightly around the bend."

Roads can also be banked, meaning one side is built higher than the other at a curve, helping vehicles turn safely at speed:

  • "The highway is banked at that corner, so vehicles can take it faster."

The underlying image is a slope — like the sloping sides of a riverbank. When something banks, it angles like that slope.
4. To keep a fire burning slowly by covering it

To bank a fire is to cover it with ash, coal dust, or heavy fuel so that it burns very slowly — just alive, not blazing — often overnight. The goal is to keep hot coals that can be easily revived in the morning.

  • "She banked the fire before going to bed so the house would stay warm."
  • "He banked the furnace each evening."
  • "The cook banked the kitchen stove so breakfast could be made quickly at dawn."

A banked fire is deliberately low and controlled, not extinguished. This was an essential daily practice before central heating existed, and you still see this meaning in literature, historical fiction, and descriptions of traditional life.
5. To pile up / to heap up ("bank up")

Things bank up when they accumulate into a thick mass or pile — the way snow, sand, clouds, or even traffic can gather and heap against something.

  • "Snow banked up against the side of the house overnight."
  • "Dark clouds were banking on the horizon — a storm was coming."
  • "Sand had banked up along the fence over the weeks."
  • "Work banked up while she was on holiday." (figurative — meaning it piled up)

This sense is close to the image of a river bank: a raised ridge that has built up naturally. When things bank up, they form a similar mass.
6. To play a shot by bouncing it off a surface (billiards, pool, some sports)

In billiards, snooker, or pool, to bank a ball means to deliberately hit it so it bounces off the cushion (the padded rail at the edge of the table) and travels toward the pocket or target.

  • "He banked the ball off the far cushion and potted it cleanly."
  • "That was a brilliant bank shot."
  • "She banked it into the corner pocket."

The same idea appears in basketball (banking a shot off the backboard) and other sports where you play a ball off a surface:

  • "He banked the shot off the backboard and it dropped in."
How often will you encounter each meaning?

Very common (everyday speech and writing):

  • Meaning 2 — bank on (rely on something) — you'll hear this constantly.
  • Meaning 1 — depositing/using a bank — also everyday.

Common in specific contexts:

  • Meaning 3 — aircraft/vehicles banking — appears regularly in descriptions of travel, news, and flying.
  • Meaning 5 — banking up (piling up) — common in weather reports, descriptions of nature, and figurative language.

Encountered in literature, history, and traditional contexts:

  • Meaning 4 — banking a fire — less common in modern conversation but frequent in older writing and historical settings.

Domain-specific:

  • Meaning 6 — banking a shot — specific to billiards, pool, and certain sports commentary.
One thing that ties it all together

Every meaning of "bank" as a verb involves either accumulation (piling up, depositing, storing) or tilting/angling (leaning into a curve, bouncing off a surface at an angle). Once you see that, the word feels much less scattered. You're always either gathering something to one side, or moving along a slope.
1465:
"Bank on" is a phrasal verb that means to rely on, trust, or feel very confident about something or someone. When you "bank on" something, you are so sure about it that you are willing to make plans or decisions based on it.

Think of it this way: when you put your money in a bank, you trust the bank completely. You are confident your money is safe and will be there when you need it. The phrase "bank on" borrows this exact idea — trusting something so much that you are willing to stake something on it.
The Core Idea in One Sentence
To bank on something = to count on it happening, or to count on someone doing something.

The phrase has its roots in the world of finance and banking. Historically, a bank was seen as the most reliable and secure place to store something valuable. So, to "bank on" something came to mean placing your full trust in it, just as you'd place your money in a bank for safekeeping. If you bank on something, you are essentially "depositing your confidence" in it.

"Bank on" always needs an object after it — something or someone that you are trusting. Here are the most common structures:

1. Bank on + a noun/pronoun
You trust a person or thing.

"You can bank on her."
"We're banking on the good weather."

2. Bank on + a gerund (verb + -ing)
You trust that a certain action or event will happen.

"I'm banking on winning the contract."
"Don't bank on getting a seat — it's usually fully booked."

3. Bank on + a noun phrase

"She banked on her years of experience to impress the panel."

Here are sentences that show how the phrase feels in natural, everyday English:

  1. "You can bank on James to get the work done. He has never let anyone down."

(James is completely trustworthy and reliable.)

  1. "Don't bank on the bus arriving on time — it's almost always late."

(It would be a mistake to trust that the bus will be punctual.)

  1. "She's banking on a salary raise to cover her new apartment's rent."

(She is confident — perhaps too confident — that the raise will happen, and she's making plans around it.)

  1. "We banked on the supplier delivering the goods early, and it worked out perfectly."

(We trusted and planned around an early delivery, and it happened.)

  1. "I wouldn't bank on it."

(A very common short expression meaning: "I wouldn't be so confident about that." It is often used as a polite or cautious warning.)

This is important. "Bank on" carries a sense of high confidence or strong expectation. It is stronger than just hoping for something. When you bank on something, you are not merely wishing — you are counting on it and possibly even planning around it.

Compare these:

  • "I hope it doesn't rain." → Just a wish. No strong expectation.
  • "I expect it won't rain." → A reasonable prediction.
  • "I'm banking on it not raining." → You are so confident it won't rain that you have made firm plans (like an outdoor picnic) based on that assumption.

Very often, "bank on" is used in negative or cautionary sentences to warn someone not to be overconfident:

  • "Don't bank on it." — Don't assume it will happen.
  • "I wouldn't bank on that if I were you." — That is risky to count on.
  • "You can't bank on the market staying stable." — It is unwise to depend on that.

This is one of the most natural uses of the phrase in everyday conversation.

These phrases are close in meaning:

PhraseNuance
  • "Count on" — Almost identical to "bank on." Very interchangeable. "You can count on me."
  • "Rely on" — Also very similar, but slightly more formal. "We rely on your support."
  • "Depend on" — Similar, and also suggests a need, not just confidence. "I depend on my morning coffee."
  • "Bet on" — More casual and informal. Implies an element of risk, like a gamble. "I'd bet on him winning."

Among these, "bank on" sits in the middle — it is informal enough for everyday conversation, but confident enough to suggest near-certainty, not just a casual preference.

Do not confuse "bank on" with "bank at", which has a completely different meaning:

  • "I bank at Barclays." = I have a bank account at Barclays. (It's about your financial institution.)
  • "I'm banking on Barclays to approve my loan." = I am trusting and depending on Barclays to say yes. (It's about confidence and reliance.)

The preposition changes the meaning entirely.

• Meaning: To rely on or feel very confident about something or someone.
  • Origin: From the idea of trusting a bank with your money.
  • Tone: Informal, conversational, used in everyday English.
  • Strength: Stronger than hoping; implies confident expectation and planning.
  • Most common use: Both positive ("You can bank on him.") and cautionary ("Don't bank on it.").

Now you know "bank on" inside and out — not just what it means, but where it came from, how it feels, how to build sentences with it, and how not to confuse it with similar words. You can bank on that knowledge serving you well!
1466:
To bankroll something means to provide the money needed to make it happen. When you bankroll a project, a business, a film, a person, or any kind of venture, you are the financial force behind it — you are putting up the cash that allows it to exist or move forward.

Think of it this way: many things in life have a great idea at the front and a wallet at the back. The person or organisation holding that wallet — the one making it all financially possible — is the one doing the bankrolling.
A Closer Look at What It Really Means

Bankrolling is not just about giving a little money here and there. It implies being the main or significant financial backer. The word carries the sense of someone stepping in and saying, "I will fund this." It suggests a sizeable, meaningful financial commitment — enough that without it, the thing being funded probably wouldn't happen at all, or couldn't continue.

For example:

  • A wealthy investor bankrolls a young entrepreneur's tech startup.
  • A movie studio bankrolls a big-budget film.
  • A government bankrolls a scientific research programme.
  • A rich parent bankrolls their child's music career.

In each case, the bankroller is the financial engine. They are not just contributing — they are carrying the financial weight.

When someone bankrolls something, there is almost always a relationship of power and dependence involved. The person or thing being bankrolled relies on the bankroller's money to survive or succeed. This gives the bankroller a certain degree of influence, control, or at the very least, a stake in the outcome.

This is why the word is often used in journalism and public discourse with a slightly suspicious or probing tone. When a reporter writes, "Who is bankrolling this political campaign?", the question is not just asking about money — it is asking about who has power over it, who has an interest in its success, and what they might want in return. The word subtly hints that the financial backer may have motives, influence, or expectations attached to their money.

That said, bankrolling is not inherently negative. It is often completely neutral or even admirable — as in a charity that bankrolls medical research, or a mentor who bankrolls a promising student's education. The connotation depends entirely on the context.
How It Is Used in Sentences

The verb follows normal grammatical patterns. Here are examples across different contexts so you can see how naturally it fits into language:

Active form (subject does the bankrolling):

  • "Her uncle bankrolled the entire restaurant venture."
  • "The corporation has been bankrolling local politicians for years."
  • "He couldn't afford to tour, so his record label bankrolled him."

Passive form (subject receives the bankrolling):

  • "The documentary was bankrolled by a Silicon Valley billionaire."
  • "The project is bankrolled by the European Union."
  • "His lifestyle was entirely bankrolled by his family's fortune."
How It Differs from Similar Words

You may wonder how bankroll is different from words like fund, finance, or sponsor. The differences are subtle but real.

Fund and finance are more formal and technical. They are used in official documents, business reports, and academic writing. They describe the act of providing money without carrying much personality or implied drama.

Sponsor leans toward a more public, branding-oriented relationship — a company sponsors an event because their logo goes on the banner and people associate them with it. There is usually a visible, marketing-driven exchange.

Bankroll, on the other hand, is more informal and vivid. It is the word journalists, storytellers, and everyday speakers reach for when they want to convey that someone is the money behind something — sometimes visibly, sometimes quietly, sometimes with strings attached. It paints a more human and dynamic picture than the drier alternatives.

Anything that requires money to exist can be bankrolled — a film, a war, a political movement, a criminal operation, a football club, a fashion line, a friend's wild business idea. The word is flexible and works across all these contexts. What stays constant is the core image: someone opening their wallet wide enough to make something else possible.

If you remember one thing, let it be this — to bankroll is to be the financial backer that makes something happen. It suggests significant funding, a degree of power or influence, and often, a reason for providing that money in the first place.
1467:
Bankrupt means being completely and officially unable to pay back the money you owe to others. Not just struggling with money, not just running low — but having reached a point where you simply cannot pay your debts at all, and this has been formally recognized, usually by a court of law.

Think of it this way: if you borrowed money from ten different people and you have no way to repay any of them — no savings, no income, no assets left — you are bankrupt.
It Is a Legal Status, Not Just a Feeling

This is one of the most important things to understand. "Bankrupt" is not just a casual way of saying someone is poor or short on cash. It is a formal, legal condition that is officially declared, usually through a court process. When a person or a business is declared bankrupt, the law steps in to manage the situation — often by selling whatever assets they have left to pay back as much of the debt as possible.

So when you say someone is bankrupt, you are describing an official state of financial collapse, not just a bad month.
Who or What Can Be Bankrupt?

Both people and organizations (companies, businesses, even governments) can be bankrupt.

A person can be bankrupt — for example, someone who took out large loans, lost their job, and has no remaining way to repay what they owe.

A company can be bankrupt — for example, a business that spent more than it earned for years, borrowed heavily, and can no longer meet its financial obligations.

In both cases, the key elements are the same: debts exist, and there is a total inability to pay them.
The Degree Matters — It Is Extreme

"Bankrupt" sits at the far end of a scale. Compare these stages:

Someone who is tight on money is just having a rough time financially. Someone who is broke (an informal word) has very little or no money right now. Someone who is in debt owes money but may still be managing it. But someone who is bankrupt has gone past all of those — they have collapsed financially to the point where repayment is impossible, and the law has to get involved.

This is why the word carries weight and seriousness. It is not used lightly.

Here is where the word becomes even more interesting and widely useful. "Bankrupt" is very commonly used in a figurative sense, meaning completely lacking something valuable — not money, but a quality, a principle, or an idea.

Just as financial bankruptcy means having nothing left to pay with, figurative bankruptcy means having nothing left of something important.

Examples:

"The politician's speech was morally bankrupt." — This means the speech had absolutely no moral integrity. It was completely empty of ethical value.

"Their argument is intellectually bankrupt." — The argument has no sound reasoning whatsoever. It holds no logical value at all.

"The regime was spiritually bankrupt." — It had completely lost any sense of higher purpose, meaning, or humanity.

Notice the pattern: when you use "bankrupt" figuratively, you are always saying that something is completely drained of or utterly devoid of a particular quality. It signals total absence, not just a shortage.
Connotation — What the Word Feels Like

"Bankrupt" carries a strong negative connotation. Whether used literally or figuratively, it signals failure, collapse, and a kind of exhaustion of resources. When used about a person financially, it can carry stigma, though in modern times many people understand that bankruptcy can happen due to circumstances beyond one's control. When used figuratively (e.g., "morally bankrupt"), it is often used to criticize harshly — it is a strong, damning judgment.
How to Use It in Sentences

Literal uses:

"The company was declared bankrupt after years of losses."
"He went bankrupt when the real estate market crashed."
"The bankrupt firm's assets were sold to pay its creditors."

Figurative uses:

"Critics called the new policy ethically bankrupt."
"A leadership that ignores its own people is morally bankrupt."
"Their creativity has become bankrupt — every idea is recycled."
How It Compares to Similar Words

Insolvent is the closest technical synonym in the financial sense — it also means unable to pay debts. However, "insolvent" is more of a dry, technical/legal term used by lawyers and accountants. "Bankrupt" is broader — it is used both in legal contexts and in everyday language, and crucially, it extends figuratively in a way "insolvent" does not.

Poor and broke simply describe a lack of money and do not carry the legal or extreme sense of "bankrupt."

Ruined is emotionally similar but vague — "bankrupt" is far more precise.

If you ever need to recall this word quickly: bankrupt means completely and officially unable to pay what you owe — and by extension, completely devoid of something valuable, whether that is money, morality, ideas, or integrity.
1468: Bankruptcy is a legal status — officially recognized by a court of law — in which a person or organization is formally declared unable to repay the money they owe to others. It is not about being temporarily tight on cash. It means the financial situation has become so overwhelmed by debt that repaying what is owed is genuinely impossible, even in the foreseeable future. When this point is reached, the person or organization can go to a court and formally declare: "I cannot pay my debts." This triggers a structured legal process that decides what happens next, fairly and in an orderly way.
The Key People Involved

Three roles are central to every bankruptcy case. The debtor is the person or organization that owes money and has entered the bankruptcy process. The creditor is anyone the debtor owes money to — a bank, a credit card company, a landlord, a supplier, or even a private individual. The trustee is a court-appointed official who manages the case, examines the debtor's financial situation, ensures the process is fair, and distributes any available money to creditors.
What Actually Happens When Someone Files

The moment someone files for bankruptcy, the court immediately issues what is called an automatic stay. This is a legal freeze that instantly stops all creditors from taking any collection actions — no more demand letters, no phone calls, no lawsuits, no repossessions — at least while the case is being resolved. This gives the debtor some breathing room to participate in the process without being hounded.

From there, what happens depends on which type of bankruptcy is filed.
Insolvency vs. Bankruptcy — An Important Distinction

These two words are often confused, so it is worth separating them clearly. Insolvency is the financial condition of being unable to pay your debts — it is purely about your financial state and can exist quietly, without anyone else knowing. Bankruptcy, on the other hand, is the formal legal process that follows when an insolvent person or organization goes to court to have that condition officially recognized and dealt with. In short: insolvency is the problem; bankruptcy is the legal response to that problem.
Voluntary vs. Involuntary Bankruptcy

Bankruptcy can be initiated in two ways. Voluntary bankruptcy is by far the most common — the debtor themselves chooses to file, deciding that the legal process is the best way to deal with an impossible debt situation. Involuntary bankruptcy, on the other hand, is when creditors petition the court to force a debtor into bankruptcy because the debtor owes them money and refuses to pay or has become clearly unable to. Courts are generally careful about granting involuntary petitions and require creditors to meet strict conditions before doing so.
The Main Types of Bankruptcy

In the United States — which has one of the most developed bankruptcy systems in the world — the types of bankruptcy are referred to by chapter numbers from the federal law. The most common are Chapter 7, Chapter 11, and Chapter 13. Other countries have their own equivalent systems with different names, but the core ideas are broadly similar worldwide.

Chapter 7 is known as liquidation bankruptcy. A trustee is appointed to sell off the debtor's non-exempt assets (more on exemptions shortly), and the money raised is distributed among creditors. Most remaining eligible debts are then discharged — meaning legally wiped away. The debtor loses many possessions but gets a clean financial slate. This is commonly used by individuals with little income and substantial unsecured debt, such as credit card balances or medical bills.

Chapter 11 is known as reorganization bankruptcy and is primarily used by businesses. Rather than shutting down entirely, the business proposes a plan to restructure its debts — negotiating lower payments, extended timelines, or reduced amounts owed — while continuing to operate. Airlines, large retailers, and major corporations have used Chapter 11 when they were in serious financial trouble but believed the business could survive with restructuring.

Chapter 13 is a repayment plan designed for individuals who have a regular income. Instead of liquidating assets, the debtor proposes a plan to repay all or part of their debts over three to five years, often at reduced amounts. This is especially useful for people who want to keep their home or car while catching up on overdue payments.
What Gets Discharged — and What Doesn't

When a debt is discharged, the debtor is no longer legally obligated to pay it, and creditors can never legally come after them for it again. This is the "fresh start" that bankruptcy promises. However, not all debts can be discharged, and this is one of the most critical things to understand.

Debts that typically cannot be wiped away include student loans (in most circumstances in the US), child support and alimony, most tax debts owed to the government, debts arising from fraud or deliberate wrongdoing, and criminal fines or penalties. These survive bankruptcy completely intact — the debtor must still pay them in full, no matter what.
Exempt Assets — What You Get to Keep

Bankruptcy does not mean losing absolutely everything you own. Exemptions are legal protections that shield certain categories of assets from being seized and sold to pay creditors. The exact exemptions vary by country and, in the US, by state — but they commonly include a portion of the value of your primary home (called a homestead exemption), a vehicle up to a certain value, basic household goods and clothing, tools you need to do your job, and certain retirement accounts. The underlying idea is that the legal system does not want to leave debtors completely destitute with nothing to rebuild from.
The Consequences of Bankruptcy

Filing for bankruptcy has real and lasting consequences beyond the courtroom.

The most significant is the damage to your credit score — the numerical rating that tells lenders how trustworthy you are as a borrower. A Chapter 7 bankruptcy stays on your credit report for ten years, while a Chapter 13 typically stays for seven. During this period, getting approved for loans, mortgages, credit cards, or even rental apartments becomes very difficult, as lenders view you as a high-risk borrower. Interest rates, if you do get approved for credit, will often be much higher than normal.

Bankruptcy is also a public record, meaning it can be looked up by employers, landlords, or anyone who searches for it. This can affect your ability to get jobs that involve financial responsibility, or to rent a home from a landlord who checks backgrounds.

There can also be social stigma attached to bankruptcy, as some people associate it with personal failure or irresponsibility — though this perception is often unfair, since many bankruptcies are caused by circumstances beyond a person's control, such as sudden medical emergencies, job loss, or economic collapse.

That said, bankruptcy is very deliberately designed to allow for recovery. Many individuals and businesses have successfully rebuilt their finances and reputations after going through the process.
Bankruptcy for Businesses vs. Individuals

While individuals typically file for bankruptcy after personal financial disasters — job loss, divorce, overwhelming medical bills, or unmanageable debt — businesses file when they can no longer meet their financial obligations to suppliers, lenders, employees, or bondholders.

When a business liquidates through bankruptcy, there is a strict legal priority order for who gets paid first. Secured creditors — those whose loans are backed by collateral, such as a bank that holds a mortgage on a building — are paid before unsecured creditors, such as suppliers or credit card companies. Shareholders are usually last in line and often receive nothing. This priority order ensures the process is predictable and fair, even if no one gets everything they are owed.
The Figurative Meaning

Beyond its strict legal definition, "bankruptcy" is widely used in everyday language to describe a complete and total absence of something valuable — not just money. You will regularly hear expressions like moral bankruptcy, which describes a person, institution, or government that has completely abandoned ethical principles and has no integrity left. Similarly, intellectual bankruptcy describes arguments, ideas, or positions that are so devoid of substance or logic that they have nothing real to offer.

In this figurative sense, the word carries its core meaning — total emptiness, utter failure, an inability to produce anything of worth — and simply applies it beyond the financial world.
Real-World Examples

To make this concrete: imagine a person who loses their job, accumulates enormous medical bills after a serious illness, and falls deeply behind on credit card payments. Their income, even after recovery, will never realistically be enough to repay the full debt. They file for Chapter 7 bankruptcy. The court discharges the eligible debts, they surrender non-exempt assets, their credit takes a hit, but they are legally free of those obligations and can start rebuilding.

On the business side, both United Airlines and Delta Air Lines filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the early 2000s. Rather than shutting down, they restructured their debts, renegotiated contracts with employees and suppliers, and continued operating. Both eventually emerged from bankruptcy and went on to become financially healthy airlines again. This illustrates something important: bankruptcy, especially for businesses, does not always mean permanent failure. It can be a painful but survivable reset.
The Single-Sentence Summary

If you had to reduce "bankruptcy" to its essence: it is the formal legal process by which a court officially recognizes that a person or organization cannot repay their debts, and then oversees a fair resolution — either by wiping those debts away, reorganizing them, or creating a repayment plan — so that both the debtor and the creditors are treated as justly as the circumstances allow.
1469: A banner is something that displays a message or represents an identity — visually, through text, images, or symbols. It appears in many forms, from a physical piece of cloth to a digital graphic, but the core idea is always the same: a banner communicates something to the people who see it, loudly and visibly.
Meaning 1: A long strip of material with writing or images on it

This is the most common, everyday meaning. A banner is a long, flat piece of material — cloth, paper, or plastic — with words or pictures on it, displayed in a public place so many people can see it.

Banners in this sense are designed to be read from a distance, which is why they are usually large and use bold, clear lettering.

Examples:

  • A "Happy Birthday!" banner hung across a room at a party.
  • A "Grand Opening" banner stretched across the front of a new shop.
  • Protesters carrying banners through the streets that read "Save Our Planet."
  • Football fans holding banners in the stadium to support their team.
Meaning 2: A flag representing a group, cause, or organization

A banner can also be a flag — typically attached to a pole — that stands for something: a country, an army, a religion, a sports team, or any organized group.

In older times (and still in formal or ceremonial contexts today), armies carried banners into battle. The banner bore the symbol or colors of their group, so everyone could see who was fighting for whom. In this sense, a banner doesn't just identify a group — it represents their identity, values, and pride.

Examples:

  • Soldiers marching under their country's banner.
  • A medieval knight carrying a banner displaying his family's coat of arms.
  • A church carrying a banner with a religious image during a procession.
Meaning 3: A banner headline in a newspaper

In journalism, a banner (often called a "banner headline") is a headline that stretches across the full width of a newspaper's front page. It is the most prominent, eye-catching headline on the page — reserved for the biggest, most dramatic news of the day.

Examples:

  • After a historic event, a newspaper might display a banner that reads: "WAR ENDS" or "EARTHQUAKE DESTROYS CITY."

The connection to the other meanings is clear: just as a physical banner is large and bold and designed to grab everyone's attention, a banner headline does the same thing in print.

On the internet, a banner — most often called a "banner ad" — is a rectangular graphic or advertisement displayed on a webpage, usually running across the top, or appearing on the sides or bottom.

Example:

  • When you visit a website and see a wide rectangular image advertising a product or service — that is a banner.

They are called banners for the same reason as everything else: like a banner hung across a street, they are wide, flat, and placed where the most eyes will see them.

One of the most important and widely used figurative expressions with this word is "under the banner of [something]," which means in the name of, in support of, or as part of a particular cause or belief.

Examples:

  • "They united under the banner of freedom and equality."
  • "Many terrible things have been done under the banner of religion."
  • "The charity operates under the banner of the Red Cross."

Just as soldiers once fought under a physical banner that represented their cause, people today act "under the banner" of an idea, movement, or organization. The physical object has become a metaphor for any cause that people rally around.
A note on "banner" as an adjective

You will almost certainly encounter "a banner year" or "a banner day" in your reading — where "banner" works as an adjective meaning exceptionally good or successful.

  • "It was a banner year for the company — profits reached an all-time high."
  • "Yesterday was a banner day — everything went perfectly."

This grew naturally from the noun: just as a banner is raised high and displayed with pride, a "banner year" is one worth raising high and celebrating.

No matter the form, "banner" always carries the same underlying spirit:

A banner stands out. A banner represents something — a message, a cause, a group, a moment. A banner is meant to be seen and noticed by many people.

Whether it's a cloth sign at a birthday party, a flag on a battlefield, a headline in a newspaper, or an ad on a website — a banner is always something that says, loudly and visibly: "Look here. This matters."
1470:
A banquet is a large, formal, and elaborate meal shared by many people, held to celebrate or mark a special occasion. Think of it as far more than just eating together — it is an organized event where food, ceremony, and company all come together in a grand way.

If a regular dinner is a candle, a banquet is a chandelier.

Not every big meal is a banquet. A banquet has a distinct character, built from these qualities:

It is large. A banquet is not for a few friends around a kitchen table. It typically involves dozens, hundreds, or even thousands of guests seated together in a hall, ballroom, or grand venue.

It is formal. There is structure and ceremony to it. Guests are often dressed elegantly. Seating may be arranged. There is usually a host or an organizing body. Things follow a plan.

It is elaborate. The food served at a banquet is not simple or casual. It is carefully prepared, often served in multiple courses — perhaps a starter, soup, a main dish, and dessert — all presented with care and style.

It marks an occasion. A banquet does not happen for no reason. It is tied to something significant — a celebration, an achievement, a welcome, or a ceremony.

It often includes more than just eating. Banquets frequently feature speeches, toasts (where people raise their glasses to honor someone), awards, performances, or entertainment. The meal is the centerpiece, but the event is bigger than the food alone.

Banquets are held for occasions that call for grandeur and gathering. Common examples include:

  • State banquets, where a country's leader hosts a formal dinner for a visiting king, queen, president, or prime minister. These are among the most prestigious banquets in the world.
  • Wedding banquets, the grand meal that follows a wedding ceremony, celebrating the newly married couple with family and friends.
  • Awards banquets, where organizations honor achievements — for example, a sports league might hold an annual banquet to present trophies and recognize outstanding players.
  • Charity banquets, formal dinners organized to raise money for a cause, where guests pay to attend and donors are recognized.
  • Graduation or academic banquets, held to celebrate students completing their studies.
  • Corporate or business banquets, where a company celebrates a milestone, welcomes important clients, or rewards employees.

In all of these, the banquet is the main event — not just a side activity.

This is where many learners get confused, so let's be precise.

Banquet vs. Dinner: A dinner is simply an evening meal — it can be casual, small, and entirely ordinary. A banquet is always a significant, large, and formal affair. All banquets involve dinner, but most dinners are not banquets.

Banquet vs. Feast: A feast emphasizes abundance — a huge spread of food, eaten with great pleasure and sometimes informally. The word "feast" can describe a joyful, relaxed gathering (even a family holiday meal). A banquet, by contrast, almost always carries an element of ceremony and formality. You can have a feast without any speeches or formal structure; a banquet rarely lacks them.

Banquet vs. Party: A party is a broad social gathering for fun and celebration — it may or may not involve a proper meal. A banquet is specifically centered on a formal, multi-course meal as its defining feature.

Banquet vs. Reception: A reception is a gathering held to welcome or honor someone (often after a wedding ceremony or official event). Receptions may include food, but they are often standing events with light refreshments, not a full seated meal. A banquet is always a full, seated, elaborate meal.

These will show you how the word naturally lives in real usage:

  • The president hosted a state banquet for the visiting foreign leaders at the palace.
  • After the award ceremony, all the guests were invited to a banquet in the hotel's grand ballroom.
  • The company organized a banquet to celebrate its fiftieth anniversary, with five hundred employees in attendance.
  • The wedding banquet lasted three hours and included speeches, dancing, and a six-course meal.
  • The charity banquet raised over a million dollars for children's education.

In everyday conversation, people sometimes use "banquet" more loosely to describe any impressively large and delicious spread of food — even at home. For example, someone might say, "My grandmother cooked an absolute banquet for us!" — meaning the meal was so plentiful and wonderful it felt like a grand feast. This is not technically precise, but it is understood and accepted in casual speech. Just know that in its true, formal sense, a banquet is always an organized, ceremonial event — not just a big home-cooked meal.
A banquet is a large, formal, multi-course meal held for many people on a special occasion, typically accompanied by speeches, ceremony, and celebration.
1471: A banshee is a supernatural female spirit from Irish and Scottish Gaelic folklore. She is not a ghost of a dead person — she is a type of fairy or spirit being that exists in her own right. Her one and only purpose is to announce that someone is about to die. She does not cause the death; she simply warns of it. Think of her as a supernatural messenger of doom.

A banshee almost always appears as a woman, but folklore describes her in a few different forms:

  • A young, beautiful woman dressed in a grey or white robe, often with long, flowing hair that she combs while crying.
  • An old, haggard woman with hollow eye sockets, a single nostril, and large teeth — terrifying to look at.
  • Sometimes a middle-aged woman in between the two extremes.

These different forms are all the same banshee — the appearance simply varies depending on the tradition or the storyteller. In some accounts, she has red or pale eyes from constant weeping. In others, she wears a green dress. She is often seen near water — washing a shroud (a burial cloth) or the bloodstained armour of the person who is about to die. This washing near water is a deeply symbolic image: she is already preparing for death before it has even happened.
The wailing cry — her defining feature

The most famous and terrifying thing about a banshee is her cry. It is described as a loud, piercing, heartbreaking wail or shriek — a sound somewhere between a woman's scream and a haunting moan. The Irish called this kind of ritualistic, grief-filled crying "keening" (a traditional form of mourning wail done at funerals). The banshee's cry is essentially a supernatural version of this.

When someone hears the banshee's wail in the night, especially near their home, it means that a member of their family will soon die. The cry itself does not kill — it is purely an announcement. Some say hearing it is unbearable, not just because it is loud or frightening, but because the grief in it feels real and overwhelming, as though the banshee is genuinely mourning the person who has not yet died.

This is an important and specific detail: the banshee is attached to particular Irish families, not to just anyone. Traditionally, she is said to follow families with old Gaelic Irish surnames — particularly those beginning with "O'" or "Mac/Mc" (such as O'Brien, O'Neill, O'Connor, MacNamara, etc.). These were considered the great, ancient Irish families, and the banshee was seen as a sort of spiritual guardian or mourner tied to their bloodline.

According to the tradition, each such family had its own banshee — a specific spirit linked to that lineage across generations. When a member of that family was going to die, their banshee would appear and wail. Hearing her meant the death was inevitable; there was no stopping it.

Over time, as the tradition spread and evolved (especially among the Irish diaspora around the world), this specific family restriction loosened in popular storytelling, and banshees became more broadly thought of as death-omens in general.

Not exactly. This is a subtle but important point. The banshee is not a villain or a monster in the way people might assume. She does not hunt people, harm them, or choose who dies. She simply knows — and she mourns. In many Irish folk stories, the banshee's wailing is a sign of love or deep loyalty to the family she watches over. She grieves because she cares. She is terrifying, yes — but she is not malicious. She is more like a tragic figure: doomed to cry for others' deaths forever.

That said, there are darker versions of the story too. In some accounts, she is associated with the Washer at the Ford — a sinister figure who washes the clothes of those about to die in battle. In this form, she feels more ominous and threatening. But even then, she is a herald, not a cause.
How the word is used in modern English

Beyond mythology, the word banshee has entered everyday English as a vivid image for a person (or thing) making a horrific, ear-splitting scream or wail. You will very commonly hear or read the phrase:

"She screamed like a banshee."
"The child wailed like a banshee."
"The alarm was shrieking like a banshee."

In this modern usage, no one literally means a mythological spirit. They are simply using "banshee" as a powerful shorthand for an intensely loud, wild, uncontrolled, frightening scream. The word carries with it all the weight of that unearthly wail from the mythology, which is why it works so well as a comparison.

You might also see "banshee" used more loosely to describe anything that makes a piercing, howling sound — like wind during a storm, a speeding car's engine, or a screaming crowd.

A banshee is a supernatural wailing woman from Irish folklore who appears near a family to announce — through a bone-chilling cry — that one of its members is about to die; and in everyday modern English, the word is used to describe anyone or anything that screams or wails with an extreme, wild intensity.
1472:
Banter is playful, teasing conversation between people who are comfortable with each other. It is light-hearted, witty, and friendly — nobody is genuinely trying to hurt anyone. Think of it as a kind of verbal ping-pong where people joke around, tease each other a little, and fire clever or funny remarks back and forth.

A single clever remark is not banter. Banter is the whole exchange — the back-and-forth flow of it.

For something to be banter, it needs to have all of these qualities at the same time:

It is playful. The mood is fun and light. Nobody is being serious. The goal is to enjoy the moment, not to win an argument or make a point.

It is teasing. People gently poke fun at each other — maybe about a mistake someone made, a habit they have, or something they said earlier. The teasing has a smile behind it.

It is mutual. Banter is not a one-way performance. Both people (or everyone in the group) participate. You joke, I joke back. That flow is what makes it banter rather than just someone telling jokes.

It is affectionate. Even when the words sound a little sharp or cheeky, the feeling underneath is warm. It actually signals comfort and closeness — people banter because they feel relaxed and friendly with each other.

It is witty. Good banter tends to be clever. Quick thinking, wordplay, a well-timed observation, a funny comeback — these are the tools of banter.

Imagine two friends, Alex and Sam. Alex shows up 20 minutes late to meet Sam at a café.

Sam says: "Oh wow, you're here. I was starting to think you'd moved to a different time zone."

Alex replies: "Sorry, I was waiting for you to actually pick a café that's worth being on time for."

Sam laughs: "Fair enough."

That entire exchange is banter. Neither person is genuinely upset. The teasing is light. Both contribute to it. There is warmth in it even though the words are a little cheeky. This is exactly what banter looks and feels like.

Understanding the edges of a word is just as important as knowing its core meaning.

Banter is not an insult. An insult is meant to genuinely hurt or put someone down. Banter is never meant to hurt — and if it accidentally does, it has stopped being banter. The intent matters enormously.

Banter is not mockery or bullying. Mockery is one-sided and mean-spirited. The person being mocked does not enjoy it. In banter, both people are smiling. The moment one person feels genuinely bad or humiliated, you have crossed out of banter and into something unkind.

Banter is not small talk. Small talk is polite but neutral conversation — about the weather, a commute, weekend plans. It is not teasing and not particularly witty. Banter has a sharper, more playful edge.

Banter is not sarcasm. Sarcasm can be cold, cutting, or passive-aggressive. Banter is warm. Sometimes banter uses sarcasm as a tool, but banter itself always stays friendly.

Banter is not telling jokes. When one person tells a joke to an audience, that is different. Banter is interactive — a live, dynamic exchange, not a performance.
A Key Nuance: Relationship Determines Banter

The exact same words can be banter in one situation and offensive in another — the difference is the relationship between the people involved.

If your closest friend says, "You have absolutely no sense of direction, do you?" after you got lost, that is probably banter. You both laugh.

If a stranger says the same thing, it could feel rude or embarrassing.

This is why banter lives almost exclusively between people who know each other well — close friends, longtime colleagues, teammates, family members. The familiarity is what gives both people the confidence that no real harm is meant.

You will most often hear banter used like this:

"We had great banter." — meaning the conversation was fun, witty, and full of playful exchanges.

"There was a lot of banter going on." — describing a lively, joking atmosphere in a group.

"He's got good banter." — a genuine compliment meaning someone is fun, quick-witted, and enjoyable to talk with.

"It was just banter." — this phrase is sometimes used (and often misused) to brush off something that went too far. If something genuinely hurt someone, calling it "just banter" afterwards does not make it banter. Real banter does not need that defence.

If you want one final way to hold onto this word — banter is what happens when wit meets warmth. It is the kind of conversation that leaves people feeling good, connected, and a little more alive. It is one of the most enjoyable forms of human interaction, and recognising it — or being told you have good banter — is always a compliment.
1473:
When something is described as bantering, it means it has the quality of being playfully teasing, lightly witty, and good-humored — like a friendly back-and-forth exchange where people joke around with each other without any real harm or serious intent.

Think of two close friends sitting together, poking fun at each other's little habits, tossing jokes back and forth, laughing the whole time — nobody is hurt, nobody is angry, and the whole thing feels easy and warm. That spirit — that light, joking, teasing quality — is what "bantering" captures as an adjective.

The adjective "bantering" is used to describe:

  • Tone — the quality of a voice or piece of writing
  • Manner — the way a person carries themselves in conversation
  • Remarks or words — specific things said
  • Exchange or conversation — the overall nature of a discussion

Examples:

  • "He replied in a bantering tone."
    His tone was light and teasing, as if he were joking around rather than being serious.
  • "She made a bantering remark about his cooking."
    She said something playfully teasing about his cooking — not to genuinely insult him, but in a friendly, joking way.
  • "Their bantering conversation lasted all evening."
    All evening, they exchanged witty, playful remarks with each other — the kind where both people are enjoying the game of it.
  • "He wrote the letter in a bantering manner."
    The letter had a light, joking, teasing style to it — not formal or serious.

"Bantering" points to a very specific emotional temperature. It sits right in the sweet spot of:

  • Warm, not cold
  • Light, not heavy
  • Playful, not mean
  • Teasing, but affectionately so
  • Witty, often clever or quick
  • Easy, not forced or strained

It is the kind of quality you feel when you're around people you're comfortable with — where a little joke lands well and nobody takes anything too seriously.

This is important, because "bantering" can be confused with similar-sounding things:

BanteringNot Bantering
Playful teasing meant in good funHarsh teasing meant to genuinely hurt
Witty back-and-forth where both sides enjoy itSarcasm or mockery where one side feels small
Light and friendlyBitter, cold, or sharp
Relaxed and naturalForced humor or awkward jokes

If someone teases you with a smile and you both laugh, that is bantering. If someone teases you with the intent to embarrass or belittle you, that is not bantering — even if it looks similar on the surface.

"Bantering" often signals a relationship of ease and comfort. You don't banter with strangers in the same way you banter with old friends. When a writer describes two characters as having a bantering exchange, they're quietly telling you: these people are comfortable with each other, they enjoy each other, and there's no real tension here — just play.

For example: "Their bantering tone made it clear they had been friends for years."

This tells you — even without describing the actual content of what was said — that their conversation had that easy, teasing, warm quality that only comes with familiarity and trust.
Words That Are Similar in Meaning

If you encounter these words, they share similar territory with "bantering":

  • Playful — lighthearted and fun
  • Teasing — gently provoking, but not harshly
  • Jocular — joking and humorous in manner
  • Witty — clever and quick with humor
  • Facetious — treating something lightly; not fully serious (though this can sometimes edge toward being dismissive)

Among all of these, "bantering" is special because it specifically suggests a back-and-forth exchange — it's not just one person being funny, but a playful conversation happening between people, even if only one side of it is being described in the moment.
Bantering means characterized by a light, playful, friendly teasing quality — the kind of witty, easy tone that comes from people who enjoy joking around with each other without any ill intent.
1474:
